Tiger Woods. An American professional golfer whose 15 major championship victories and revolutionary playing style transformed golf in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries. Born in 1975, he dominated the sport from 1997 through the 2010s, becoming the most prominent athlete in golf history and the first player of multiracial descent to achieve such dominance in the sport.

He won the Masters at age 21 in 1997, his first professional major, defeating the field by 12 strokes—the largest margin in Masters history. He captured 15 major championships, closing within three of Jack Nicklaus's all-time record of 18. After an extraordinary drought without a major victory from 2008 to 2019—eleven years—Woods won the 2019 Masters to end that drought.

In February 2021, Woods suffered a near-fatal car crash that left him with multiple serious injuries. He recovered to compete professionally again, demonstrating resilience reminiscent of other great golfers who overcame adversity. He is known for his psychological intensity, aggressive style, and remarkable ability to come from behind in major tournaments. He won the PGA Championship 5 times, the US Open 3 times, and The Open Championship 3 times, in addition to his Masters titles. Woods earned an estimated 2 billion dollars in career earnings, making him one of the wealthiest athletes in history.

Jack Nicklaus, the record-holder at 18 majors, is the player against whom Woods's career is constantly measured. Phil Mickelson was a contemporary rival and fellow dominant force in early twenty-first-century golf. Rory McIlroy represents the succeeding generation of dominant players who came after Woods's era. Woods continued the elevation that Arnold Palmer pioneered, raising golf's profile globally.
